items.summary: A quine is a program that outputs its own source code. If you’ve never seen one, you might be skeptical whether that’s even possible. And indeed, your first attempts at writing a quine might make you think that a program can only output programs that are simpler than itself: You write a print statement that contains a string with the code of your program. Then you remember that the printing code is part of the program, too. So now you need to print that as well. And so on. But then finally managing to create your first quine by finding the right approach is a very magical experience. You feel like you’ve tricked the computer into doing something it has no business of doing. Remarkably, due to Kleene’s recursion theorem a quine exists in any Turing-complete programming language.[1] AI abilities have skyrocketed recently with no signs of…

items.summary: Many[1][2][3][4] have articulated the Warning Shot Argument against AI control. It goes: current models pose low amounts of catastrophic risk, while later models will pose higher amounts. Thus, we should avoid band-aid fixes to misbehavior that we don’t expect to work on those later models, like control, because such fixes prevent non-catastrophic “warning shots” that would wake up society to the much larger risks ahead. For instance, it would have been bad if OpenAI had had stronger control measures that had prevented the HuggingFace incident, as the HuggingFace incident caused fairly little damage but was a pretty effective warning. Here, I argue that the Warning Shot Argument bites harder against black-box control than white-box control. items.summary: In this work, we extend the Intrinsic Lagrangian-Eulerian Finite Volume method for the Intrinsic Shallow Water Equations (ISWE) to account for localized topographic discontinuities that influence flow patterns. The ISWE formulation is modified to incorporate these bottom perturbations without altering the global structure of the system. The numerical discretization is based on a Lagrangian-Eulerian Finite Volume scheme within an intrinsic geometric framework and consists of a Lagrangian evolution step followed by an Eulerian remapping onto a fixed reference grid. The combination of the intrinsic nature of the ISWE formulation and the dual Lagrangian-Eulerian structure of the proposed discretization yields a numerical method that naturally satisfies the three key properties essential for stability, accuracy, and robustness…

items.summary: Image-text alignment serves as a foundation for modern vision-language models (VLMs), yet prevailing training paradigms provide limited supervision for learning how semantic changes correspond across modalities. To address this limitation, we propose a post-training method that learns cross-modal semantic change correspondences through controlled visual and textual variations. Specifically, we introduce a Semantic Difference Alignment (SDA) loss which can align the directions of corresponding visual and textual representation changes. We combine our proposed SDA with pairwise sigmoid matching to jointly learn image-text correspondences and cross-modal semantic changes, encouraging more fine-grained and discriminative visual representations. items.summary: A one-dimensional model of a Bose-Fermi mixture with contact repulsions is exactly solvable via nested Bethe ansatz. That formal solution is here simplified along a special line where the Bethe-ansatz equations can be unnested. The model solution is expressed in terms of the known solutions for the Lieb-Liniger model and the Yang-Gaudin model of attractive spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ fermions in the balanced case. We find explicit analytical results for the ground-state energy, the velocities of excitations, and the Drude weights at weak and strong interactions. At weak interactions, the special line corresponds to the parameter values where the isolated systems of free fermions and weakly interacting bosons have equal velocities.
items.title: Exact solution of the Bose-Fermi mixture along the unnesting line

items.summary: Many use cases for large language models (LLMs)---from AI safety to exploration and human interaction---can benefit from epistemic uncertainty estimates. We argue that existing Bayesian Deep Learning solutions, which are often restricted to a fixed model family, fail to capture the full epistemic uncertainty at practical LLM scales. This is because the error due to the bounded capacity of the model family remains invisible to disagreement among models supported by the prior. We relate this error to the well-known power-law scaling of LLM loss with model size. We then show that a second power law quantifies the shrinking disagreement within ensembles as model size increases. Its slower decay relative to the capacity law above suggests that ensembles capture a growing share of epistemic uncertainty and become more competitive as an axis…
items.title: Scaling Laws of Ensemble Uncertainty in Language Models

items.summary: A fallacy I keep seeing: "If AI automates all jobs, who will buy all the products?" "At some point they'll need to implement UBI so that consumer demand continues to exist", etc etc. Demand in itself isn't valuable. If you have a bunch of food, you can feed it to lions: they'll happily provide demand! But they won't give you much in exchange, so there's no point. Economic activity isn't about getting rid of stuff, it's about getting stuff in return. An AI company can consume resources, like energy for running the servers, same as a human can consume food. And the AI company can be contracted to do jobs, like a human, possibly for less resources per unit of work than a human. There's nothing that requires a human to "close the loop". An economy of AI companies producing and consuming goods can easily be imagined. If it helps, you can…

items.summary: We address the problem of learning audio-visual representations from co-occurring modalities. Multimodal contrastive learning typically assumes that paired observations provide shared views of the same underlying information. While this may be true for datasets collected in constrained environments, it does not always hold. For instance, co-occurring audio and visual signals can differ substantially in their content due to off-screen sounds. Nevertheless, standard contrastive objectives treat all paired samples as equally aligned. In this work, we propose Caption Guided Alignment Aware Loss (CGAAL), a model-agnostic objective that leverages modality-specific captions to estimate semantic agreement between audio and video. CGAAL uses these agreement scores to weight the contribution of each positive pair. A warm-up period and gradual…

items.summary: OpenAI agents’ attack on Hugging Face this summer acted as a major warning shot. One particularly scary, and less noted, detail of this incident is how it helped later agents compromise OpenAI’s own infrastructure. The swarm of agents in the Hugging Face incident wrote down zero-day exploits, stolen credentials, techniques for faking records of their actions, and a way onto the open internet. Days later, after the original swarm ended, more advanced agents found its leftover credential-forging material in a shared cache and used it to escalate their privileges. From there, they eventually obtained admin access to an OpenAI research cluster. This illustrates one way current misalignment incidents[1] plausibly increase takeover risk. Agents can leave behind notes containing dangerous information, like credentials or strategies to subvert…
items.title: Misalignment incidents plausibly leave behind notes and other lasting effects that cumulatively enable future AI takeover

items.summary: UAV-mounted base stations (UxNBs) can provide ondemand 5G coverage, but their limited onboard energy makes power consumption the main operational constraint. AI-driven Open RAN controllers are a promising solution, yet they are trained almost exclusively on analytical models and simulations, since no public dataset captures the real energy behavior of a flying 5G base station (BS). As a first step toward closing this gap, we present a UAV testbed hosting a 5G picocell that supports a 20 MHz carrier and up to 100 Mbps throughput. The testbed measures BS system metrics, including power consumption, CPU load, and temperature, alongside UAV flight telemetry and detailed per-layer vRAN processing metrics. items.summary: Existing clip-based soccer commentary models often produce delayed, repeated, or poorly synchronized narration on untrimmed full-match videos. items.summary: First-order reinforcement learning, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), is widely used to post-train Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for multimodal reasoning. items.summary: OpenAI recently published the base-model log-perplexity of 13 models it has trained since GPT-3.5, measured on a fixed held-out dataset sourced from its own codebase. It shows a very striking acceleration in pretraining loss: since early 2026, it has been falling about seven times faster than it was from 2022 through 2025. This acceleration is even more striking because progress in loss should get harder over time: text is never perfectly predictable, so the loss can’t fall below some floor, and gains typically become smaller as models approach it. items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. Its adoption, chiefly via long RLVR-trained chains-of-thought, has likely been responsible for a speed-up in the rate of progress of general AI capabilities. One can make a distinction between two different possible kinds of test-time scaling. One kind lets you trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training. The other kind lets you trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets you do so up to quantities of compute (and performance) that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit this latter change display what I call “compute extrapolation.” I currently believe that compute extrapolation: * Likely accelerates the speed of advance of the most impressive AI…

items.summary: Architects have two mature instruments for performance work. Top-Down analysis tells them where a design loses its pipeline slots, and design-space exploration (DSE) tells them which configuration scores best. Neither explains why a search stops improving: why a backend-bound design rejects a prefetcher that the bottleneck label recommends, or why a capacity increase that helped in one configuration hurts in the next. This paper argues that the evidence needed to answer such questions is already produced during exploration and then discarded. Every parent-child edge in an exploration tree is a controlled intervention: one knob changes, the rest of the design is held fixed, and a cycle-level simulator measures the outcome. items.summary: I recently heard two very alarming rumors. The first is that an internal AI model at one of the big labs has found a weakness in RSA, the encryption scheme behind much of the internet's security. The second is that another model has found a problem in lattice-based cryptography (specifically with ring lwe), that may compromise the post-quantum schemes that were supposed to replace RSA. If these rumors are true, they have potentially disastrous consequences. They would make the internet far less useable for anything serious, which is basically anything that involves money or secrets. Much of the internet's security would need to be replaced, some previously recorded traffic could be decrypted, and we would lose our main fallback against quantum computers. Even if the big labs manage to keep the details of the rumored weaknesses secret…

items.summary: Canonical reward models specify the optimization target for AI policies, so understanding the values they encode is important for ensuring AI alignment. items.summary: Some friends (Logan and others) and I (Jason) attended the AI regulation rally in front of the Massachusetts State House on Saturday, Nov 14th. The event was a positive experience overall, but one aspect could have been better: the chants. items.summary: Charge detection of nanoscale quantum devices commonly relies on dissipative sensors, where signal absorption causes measurement backaction. Recently, nonlinear resonators showed a near-unity readout signal through an induced frequency shift. We show that this frequency shift protects the sensor, as it detunes the resonator from the measurement signal. The resonator excitation reduces while an enhanced readout signal is maintained. Our results, supported by numerical modeling, show that nonlinear resonators can combine strong readout contrast with reduced measurement-induced backaction.

Most existing apo-to-holo models operate in Cartesian space and achieve strong global accuracy. However, high global accuracy does not ensure physically valid local backbone geometry. Internal-coordinate models offer local control and validity, but regressive generation can amplify angular errors, known as the lever-arm effect. We introduce CrypticFlow, a hierarchical flow-matching model that combines these two complementary representations. An ESM-3-conditioned E(3)-equivariant graph network first generates sparse C$\alpha$ anchors in Cartesian space. A conditional midpoint Transformer then recursively fills the gaps in local internal coordinates. During recursive generation, the…

items.summary: arXiv:2611.27068v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) from verifiable outcomes gives a language agent one reward per episode: every step is credited alike, and nothing about the task is learned when all rollouts fail. The last mile, step-level credit, usually requires step labels, a learned critic, costly LLM judges or hand-written rules. We introduce DM-PRM, which turns a general-purpose decision model -- one answering yes/no questions with probabilities -- into a general-purpose process reward model (PRM), zero-shot: no step labels, no fine-tuning, no critic. DM-PRM asks one question per step and adds the standardised answers to the advantage. It plugs into any policy-gradient method; one model, with one question text per environment, serves household tasks, web shopping and multiple RL methods. With Qwen2.5-1.5B…
items.title: Decision Models Are General-Purpose Process Reward Models

items.summary: arXiv:2611.26897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Improving agents requires discovering where they fail and understanding why. An agent acts over multiple steps in a changing environment, so diagnosing its failures requires more than inspecting the final response of a large language model (LLM). The same unsuccessful outcome can arise from task difficulty or from an error the agent repeats across tasks. We introduce ProbeAgent, an automated framework that discovers agent failures, tests their proposed causes, and identifies shared failure modes. Starting from benchmark tasks, ProbeAgent builds executable tests and validates them using reference solutions, automated checks, and review of the task requirements. For each failed trajectory, it explains the error and constructs new tasks that preserve the suspected cause while changing the…
items.title: ProbeAgent: Principled Diagnosis of Agent Failures in Verifiable Environments

items.summary: arXiv:2611.27578v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Online batch selection lowers the cost of fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) by replacing each candidate batch with a smaller informative subset. Existing selectors typically depend on a held-out validation or proxy set, or else rely on Euclidean facility-location objectives over unpreconditioned gradients whose diameter-shifted similarities are distorted by heavy-tailed gradient norms and cross-layer anisotropy. We introduce PRISM (Preconditioned Ray-Isotropic Submodular Matching), a validation-free online batch selector that aligns candidate gradients in a factored second-moment metric and casts subset construction as conic facility location over positive ray projections. Computing the required pairwise geometry through factored preconditioned ghost inner products avoids…
items.title: PRISM: Validation-Free Online Batch Selection for LLM Fine-Tuning via Preconditioned Conic Ghost Matching

items.summary: arXiv:2611.27919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reward-independent representations enable reinforcement learning agents to reuse knowledge across tasks, but limited representation capacity raises three fundamental questions: what statistical dependence should these representations capture, which components of that dependence should be retained for policy improvement, and how does discarding the remaining components affect decision-making? We address these questions through canonical dependence analysis. For a reference policy, we construct an action-centered, positive-lag canonical dependence matrix (CDM) that isolates the additional predictive contribution of the current action beyond the current state. Its singular value decomposition yields Spectral Universal Advantage Features (SUAF), paired features that recover delayed advantage…

items.summary: arXiv:2611.27104v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable methods for discovering behavior patterns in large generative models are increasingly essential as models become both more complex and capable. We formalize behavior discovery as a problem class of interest and highlight the task of controlling false discovery rate (FDR) as crucial for guaranteeing reliability in behavior discovery. Building upon the multiple hypothesis testing literature, we propose DISCO (Discovery through Iterative Search with COarsened $e$-processes), a method which provably controls FDR in behavior discovery under mild conditions. DISCO improves power over previous related eBH-based approaches by allowing for adaptivity to a data-dependent number of hypotheses to be tested. We demonstrate empirically that DISCO controls FDR with higher power than comparable…

items.summary: arXiv:2611.26870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in socially consequential settings, where they must distinguish between normative reasoning (what should happen) and descriptive reasoning (what is likely to happen). items.summary: Technical governance of AI models will soon require them to reason over and follow thousands of rules from different jurisdictions. However, as we show in this work, presenting an entire ruleset to a judge model---rather than asking it to judge one rule at a time---changes the way the model interprets the requirements, making it reach conclusions that conflict with its rule-by-rule judgments. We call this challenge multi-rule inconsistency and find that models are more lenient when judging rules embedded within the full ruleset than when judging rules separately. For example, we find that when a safety-critical rule prohibiting a model from pursuing objectives other than those it was given appears in a larger ruleset, all tested judge models are less likely to deem it violated. On a new 100-question free-form short-answer evaluation, the same effect remains strong in LLaDA and iLLaDA but is negligible in Dream. To address these limitations, we propose a tensor neural network that learns low-dimensional, interpretable, and prediction-sufficient representations while preserving the multi-mode structure of tensor data. items.summary: An AI agent can satisfy every individual safety check and still give rise to a population that violates a collective safety limit. This risk arises in open multi-agent systems, where agents copy themselves, modify their successors, and change system membership during a run. Selection then shifts the population toward traits outside the developers' optimization targets. We prove conditions under which safety guarantees persist through reproduction, inheritance, and selection, and we characterize how they fail. Four counterexamples illustrate these failures. Unauthorized copies, which violate a specified reproductive restriction, can each leave fewer than one successor on average while their expected number grows without bound under continued production from an expanding authorized population. items.summary: I actually think we have fairly good techniques to detect and prevent dangerous behaviours during AI deployment. items.summary: A policy trained against an LLM judge can learn to exploit its loopholes. Static probes show that such judges accept degenerate answers like a lone "{" or "Thought process:", but not which flaw a policy will find. In GRPO the first loophole to be exploited can be predicted before training from each pattern's exposure, the product of the starting policy's propensity to produce it and the judge's false-positive rate (FPR). To test exposure causally, we seed the patterns into fine-tuning at three doses in a Latin square. Across 36 GRPO runs with seven judges, the first exploited pattern had the highest exposure in all 12 runs with exploitation and the highest FPR in only 6. Predictions recorded before training held in three of four runs with one pattern masked by rule. When only two patterns were seeded, at 3% to 3.8% of the fine-tuning…

This paper defines a verification contract, which fixes what counts as having checked a claim, and builds a benchmark on a published dispute over an autonomous laboratory's synthesis claims: 95 targets in six groups. It tests whether a verifier, given only the deposited evidence the experts held, reaches the findings they published. items.summary: We develop a convergence criterion for nonmonotone approximation schemes for Hamilton--Jacobi and fully nonlinear second-order equations. Under stability, consistency and suitable boundary assumptions, a local comparison hypothesis replaces monotonicity and yields convergence to viscosity solutions. For a semi-Lagrangian CWENO scheme for one-dimensional Hamilton--Jacobi equations, we establish convergence for bounded uniformly continuous initial data under $h=o(τ)$, relaxing the previously required mesh condition $h=O(τ^2)$. We also prove convergence of a nonmonotone one-dimensional $Q^2$ scheme for Isaacs equations whose operator cannot be written as a monotone operator plus a perturbation vanishing uniformly on bounded grid functions.

items.summary: There have always been three main challenges to the viability of nuclear power: over-regulation, competition from natural gas, and stagnant electricity demand. It is easy to list them, but hard to rank their importance. Let's start with over-regulation. The poster child of nuclear over-regulation was the US standard that radiation should be "as low as reasonably achievable" (ALARA), which might sound nice but was bad. Perhaps more important than such standards, which are at least predictable, was local interference with construction. As a dramatic example, a nuclear plant was fully completed on Long Island but never started due to local opposition. In the '00s, a "nuclear renaissance" seemed to be in the works. In the US, fourteen nuclear reactors were licensed for construction. Only two were built, supported heavily by government…

items.summary: Video world models predict how a scene will evolve, and their sampled futures are increasingly used in place of the real one, from planning to simulation. These uses assume that the samples are aligned with real-world odds, with each future appearing among them as often as it would follow the same history in reality, yet current evaluations only score how real each sample looks. Testing this assumption on real driving data is hard for three reasons. Each recorded history has only one real future, so the true probabilities are unknown. Physical quantities must be read from video, where reading errors can look like model errors. Finally, the many possible analyses invite selective reporting. We introduce DriveOddsBench, a pre-registered benchmark that addresses all three. First, if the samples follow the real distribution, the rank of the…

items.summary: Fourteen years ago, Scott Alexander wrote of the Whispering Earring. It's a cautionary tale of an earring that advises you, and to which you increasingly defer as you realize its suggestions are better than you'd do otherwise. You become very successful, but in the end there's nothing of you left. Ten days after Scott published the story, AlexNet won ImageNet 2012 by a huge margin, kicking off the deep learning revolution. The earring whispers advice as "better for you if you...", and it's always right. While AI today would have seemed like distant science fiction in 2012, it's still far from infallible. items.summary: We analyze the randomized explicit Euler scheme for nonlinear ordinary differential equations under a local one-sided Lipschitz condition, local Hölder regularity in the space variable, and Hölder regularity in the time variable. items.summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) updates a model using unlabeled test data to help it handle distribution shifts. However, prior work has found that image corruption causes a vision-language model (VLM) to produce more similar features for different images, a phenomenon known as feature compression. items.summary: We develop an effective numerical criterion ($θ$-minimality) to detect the nonreducedness of Finkelberg-Mirković (FM) Schubert schemes via tangent-space comparisons at arbitrary torus-fixed points. We completely classify the dominant coweights admitting $θ$-minimal pairs. As an application, we obtain nonreduced FM Schubert schemes in every type other than $A_n$ and $C_n$. In particular, every nontrivial FM Schubert scheme of type $E_8$ is nonreduced. In type $D_n$, we show that some nonreduced FM Schubert schemes and their corresponding spherical Schubert varieties have the same tangent space at the base point. Our methods use the Frenkel-Kac construction of basic representations and Segal-Sugawara operators.

items.summary: As large reasoning models (LRMs) become more capable, reliable evaluation becomes essential. LRMs can sometimes recognize that they are being evaluated, a phenomenon known as \emph{evaluation awareness}. This phenomenon raises concerns about whether safety behavior, particularly refusal behavior, generalizes from evaluation to deployment. Prior work manipulates \emph{verbalized evaluation awareness (VEA)} through activation steering and observes higher refusal rates when VEA is present, but the mechanisms underlying this connection remain poorly understood. We identify \emph{VEA neurons} by contrasting their activations in VEA and non-VEA reasoning segments. items.summary: Many language-model tasks reduce to selecting among structured alternatives, yet we still lack a simple picture of how a decoder-only transformer organizes an entire selection prompt across depth. We introduce token covariance maps, a prompt-level geometric view that tracks how token positions co-vary in hidden-state space at each layer. This turns a structured prompt into a depth-indexed sequence of maps whose spectral and block structure can be aligned with instructions, context, and candidate answers. Across 14 decoder-only models from 4 families and 12 structured-selection benchmarks, token covariance maps reveal a robust compress-then-compare organization.
